segments.say: Let me take you to a laboratory in Madison, Wisconsin, in the 1950s. A psychologist called Harry Harlow is running a primate research centre at the University of Wisconsin. He studies rhesus monkeys, and in the middle of a conversation among psychologists about what a baby really needs, he decides to ask the monkeys.

show.title: Two mothers made of wire and cloth

segments.say: At the time, a leading idea in psychology was that infants love their mothers because mothers feed them. It was called cupboard love. Hunger is a drive, food reduces it, and so whoever supplies the food becomes valuable. Love, on this view, was a kind of side effect of the milk.

show.sub: Love as a side effect of food

segments.say: Harlow was not convinced. He'd noticed that baby monkeys separated from their mothers became strongly attached to the cloth pads in their cages, and became upset when the pads were taken away for cleaning. That small observation suggested that comfort, not only food, was important. So he built an experiment to test it.

He created two artificial mothers. One was made of bare wire mesh, with a bottle attached to feed the baby. The other was covered in soft terrycloth, warmed by a light bulb inside, but with no food at all. Newborn monkeys, taken from their real mothers soon after birth, lived in cages with both.

show.what: Infant rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers

segments.say: If cupboard love was right, the babies should have gone to the wire mother, because she was the one with the milk. A baby monkey would feed from her and then ignore her. Anyone who held the old view would have expected the cloth mother to be a lovely but useless piece of furniture.

It didn't turn out like that. The baby monkeys spent most of their time clinging to the cloth mother, many hours each day. They visited the wire mother only briefly, to feed, and then climbed straight back to the soft one. Even the monkeys who got their milk from wire went back to cloth for comfort.

show.title: Time spent on the cloth mother
show.label: the babies clung to cloth, even when milk was on wire

segments.say: Harlow named the effect contact comfort. A baby does not need a mother only as a food dispenser. A baby needs to hold on to something warm and soft. And the reaction of the monkeys to the cloth mother suggested that touch is a deep, fundamental need, not just a pleasant extra.

That third point is the one that has stayed with many psychologists. When Harlow put a frightening object into the cage, such as a toy bear that beat a drum, the babies ran straight to the cloth mother, clung to her, and then, after a while, began to look at the strange thing with more courage.

show.title: What the monkeys showed
items: The soft mother was a place to hold on
Babies explored more when she was near
Without her, they froze in fear

segments.say: That behaviour has a name now. The cloth mother worked as what psychologists call a secure base: a person or place from which you can step out into the world and to which you can return when frightened. John Bowlby, a British psychiatrist, was developing attachment theory at the same time. Mary Ainsworth later built the research on it.

The same pattern shows up in human babies and toddlers. A child who feels safe will wander a little further, look around, try something new, and then check back with a glance at a parent. It looks like a small act of independence, but it depends on knowing that someone is there.

show.sub: A safe place to come back to

segments.say: There's something quietly beautiful in that. Security does not make children clingy in the long run. It gives them what they need to explore. Harlow's monkeys, in their strange laboratory, ran toward the cloth mother in fear, and then, after a pause, went out and looked at the world.

But the Harlow story does not end there, and it would not be honest to stop here. Harlow also ran experiments in which baby monkeys were kept in isolation for months, away from any other animals. Those monkeys grew up with serious problems. They were fearful, withdrawn, and unable to relate to others.

Monkeys raised in isolation often rocked back and forth, clutched themselves, and had great difficulty mating or caring for their own babies. These findings added to what we know about the importance of early social contact. But they also came at an enormous cost to the animals, and many people today regard them as cruel.

Partly in response to work like this, the rules for animal research changed. Many countries introduced stricter oversight, and the idea that suffering needs a very strong justification became part of the way researchers talk. Harlow's work is often cited as an example of why those rules exist.

It can feel uncomfortable to hold both of those at once, and perhaps that's right. A good way to remember a study like this is to acknowledge its insight and its cost. We can learn from history without pretending it was gentle.

show.title: Two things can be true
items: The experiments changed how we understand love
Many scientists now would not run them

segments.say: Harlow's famous paper, The Nature of Love, grew out of an address he gave in 1958. He wrote plainly that love for the mother was not simply an offshoot of feeding. It's a line that now sounds obvious, which tells you how far the idea has travelled since then.

show.what: The Nature of Love, his presidential address to the American Psychological Association

segments.say: The research on contact and attachment helped change real practices. Hospitals started allowing parents to stay with sick children. Premature babies began to be held skin to skin. Orphanages and care homes started to think seriously about steady caregivers instead of rotating shifts. Small changes that grew out of a very big question.

Today, holding a newborn against the parent's bare chest, called kangaroo care, is recommended in many hospitals, especially for premature babies. Studies have linked it to better temperature control, steadier breathing and closer bonding. It isn't magic, but it's a good example of how a laboratory insight can end up in a very ordinary room.

It's a small picture, a blanket and a toy, but it stands for the whole discovery. Before we can be brave, we need something to hold on to. For a baby, that's a parent. For an adult, it can be a person, a place or even a familiar routine at the end of a long day.

show.cap: Something soft to hold on to

segments.say: It's a nice question to take with you. Who, or what, is your cloth mother? The friend who calls you back, the room that makes you feel calm, the song you play before a stressful day. These are not childish things. They're the quiet places from which we go out into the world.

And if you notice someone around you who seems restless or frightened, you can sometimes be that for them. You don't need a speech. A steady presence, a cup of tea, a message saying you're thinking of them. Harlow's monkeys show how much those small things matter.

So what did Harlow's mothers teach us? That love isn't just a bargain for food, that comfort is a need, and that safety is the starting point for courage. They also taught us to think about the price of knowledge, and to ask whether a discovery can justify how it was made.

show.sub: What the wire and cloth taught us

segments.say: Harlow's ideas found a sad, real-world echo in the way children were cared for in some institutions in the twentieth century. Researchers later studied children raised in large orphanages with very little personal attention, and found that those who spent a long time there often had difficulties with attachment and development. The Bucharest Early Intervention Project, which followed Romanian children, found that those moved earlier into caring foster families did better on many measures than those who stayed in the institution.

What does all this come down to? Not perfection. Researchers who study attachment are quite clear that children don't need flawless parents. They need adults who are reasonably responsive, who notice them, comfort them when they are upset, and come back after a mistake. Winnicott called it being good enough. It's a modest standard, and it's a hopeful one, because most people can meet it most of the time.

In our next story, the question moves from the nursery to the street. It asks why, in a crowd, a person in trouble can sometimes be left alone, and what we really know about that famous case in New York that made the world ask the question.
